claim: Rapid eye movement sleep (REMs) is characterized by activated electroencephalogram (EEG) and muscle atonia, accompanied by vivid dreams.
source: Rapid eye movement sleep (REMs) is characterized by activated electroencephalogram (EEG) and muscle atonia, accompanied by vivid dreams.
evidence: This is a well-established characterization of REMs based on scientific consensus.

claim: REMs is homeostatically regulated, ensuring that any loss of REMs is compensated by a subsequent increase in its amount.
source: REMs is homeostatically regulated, ensuring that any loss of REMs is compensated by a subsequent increase in its amount.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the subsequent sentence.

claim: REMs is homeostatically regulated in various species including mice, rats, cats, and humans.
source: Rapid eye movement sleep (REMs) is homeostatically regulated as demonstrated in various species including mice, rats, cats, and humans (Siegel and Gordon, 1965; Beersma et al., 1990; Benington et al., 1994; Endo et al., 1997; Endo et al., 1998; Rechtschaffen et al., 1999; Franken, 2002; Shea et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: GABAergic neurons in the preoptic area of the hypothalamus projecting to the tuberomammillary nucleus (POAGAD2→TMN neurons) are crucial for the homeostatic regulation of REMs in mice.
source: Here, we show that GABAergic neurons in the preoptic area of the hypothalamus projecting to the tuberomammillary nucleus (POAGAD2→TMN neurons) are crucial for the homeostatic regulation of REMs in mice.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: POAGAD2→TMN neurons are most active during REMs.
source: POAGAD2→TMN neurons are most active during REMs, and inhibiting them specifically decreases REMs.
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Inhibiting POAGAD2→TMN neurons specifically decreases REMs.
source: POAGAD2→TMN neurons are most active during REMs, and inhibiting them specifically decreases REMs.
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic inhibition experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: REMs restriction leads to an increased number and amplitude of calcium transients in POAGAD2→TMN neurons.
source: REMs restriction leads to an increased number and amplitude of calcium transients in POAGAD2→TMN neurons, reflecting the accumulation of REMs pressure.
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data during REMs restriction shown in Figure 3.

claim: Inhibiting POAGAD2→TMN neurons during REMs restriction blocked the subsequent rebound of REMs.
source: Inhibiting POAGAD2→TMN neurons during REMs restriction blocked the subsequent rebound of REMs.
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic inhibition experiments during REMs restriction shown in Figure 4.

claim: The POA contains neurons that become activated during sleep and that are sufficient and necessary for sleep.
source: The POA contains neurons that become activated during sleep and that are sufficient and necessary for sleep (Economo, 1930; Nauta, 1946; McGinty and Sterman, 1968; Sallanon et al., 1989; Sherin et al., 1996; Szymusiak et al., 1998; Lu et al., 2000; Gong et al., 2004; Takahashi et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2015; Kroeger et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: POA GABAergic neurons projecting to the tuberomammillary nucleus form a subpopulation of sleep-active POA neurons.
source: Specifically, POA GABAergic neurons projecting to the tuberomammillary nucleus (POAGAD2→TMN neurons) form a subpopulation of sleep-active POA neurons, and promote sleep when optogenetically activated (Chung et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: POAGAD2→TMN neurons promote sleep when optogenetically activated.
source: Specifically, POA GABAergic neurons projecting to the tuberomammillary nucleus (POAGAD2→TMN neurons) form a subpopulation of sleep-active POA neurons, and promote sleep when optogenetically activated (Chung et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: c-Fos expression in the POA is increased in REMs restricted rats.
source: A previous study demonstrated that c-Fos expression in the POA is increased in REMs restricted rats (Gvilia et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The calcium activity of POAGAD2→TMN neurons was significantly higher during REMs compared with that during wake and NREMs.
source: The calcium activity of POAGAD2→TMN neurons was significantly higher during REMs compared with that during wake and NREMs (Figure 1B and C; detailed statistical results are shown in Figure legends and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: The calcium activity of POAGAD2→TMN neurons during NREMs→REMs transitions becomes significantly increased 40 s before the REMs onset and remains elevated throughout REMs.
source: We found that the calcium activity of POAGAD2→TMN neurons during NREMs→ REMs transitions becomes significantly increased 40 s before the REMs onset and remains elevated throughout REMs (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: During NREMs→wake transitions, the activity of POAGAD2→TMN neurons started rising 10 s before the wake onset and remained elevated for 10 s after the onset.
source: During NREMs→wake transitions, the activity of POAGAD2→TMN neurons started rising 10 s before the wake onset and remained elevated for 10 s after the onset (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The ΔF/F activity of POAGAD2→TMN neurons gradually increased throughout NREMs episodes.
source: The ΔF/F activity gradually increased throughout NREMs episodes (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The activity of POAGAD2→TMN neurons is preceded by an increase in the θ and σ power and reduction in the δ power.
source: We found that the activity of POAGAD2→TMN neurons is preceded by an increase in the θ and σ power and reduction in the δ (0.5–4.5 Hz) power (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by spectrotemporal correlation analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: POAGAD2→TMN axonal fibers were most active during REMs.
source: Similar to the activity found for POAGAD2→TMN neurons using retrograde AAVs (Figure 1B and C), POAGAD2→TMN fibers were most active during REMs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data of axonal fibers shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: During NREMs, the activity of POAGAD2→TMN axonal fibers gradually increased before transitioning to REMs.
source: During NREMs, the activity of POAGAD2→TMN axonal fibers gradually increased before transitioning to REMs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), demonstrating that the activity of POAGAD2→TMN axonal fibers closely resembles that of cell bodies.
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: TMNHIS neurons are highly active during wake and less active during NREMs and REMs.
source: Consistent with previous electrophysiological studies (Steininger et al., 1999; Vanni-Mercier et al., 2003; John et al., 2004; Takahashi et al., 2006), we found in photometry recordings that TMNHIS neurons are highly active during wake and less active during NREMs and REMs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C and citations to prior research.

claim: The activity of TMNHIS neurons became significantly activated after the transition from NREMs or REMs to wakefulness.
source: Consistent with this, the activity of TMNHIS neurons became significantly activated after the transition from NREMs or REMs to wakefulness (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The TMNHIS neuron activity gradually decreased during NREMs episodes.
source: The TMNHIS neuron activity gradually decreased during NREMs episodes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E), possibly as a result of inhibitory inputs from POAGAD2→TMN neurons (Chung et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E and a citation to prior research.

claim: TMNHIS neuron activity gradually decreases throughout the inter-REM interval, reaching its lowest level at the onset of REMs.
source: Moreover, examining the time course of TMNHIS neurons between two successive REMs episodes (inter-REM interval), we found that their activity gradually decreases throughout the inter-REM interval, reaching its lowest level at the onset of REMs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F.

claim: A minimal activity of TMNHIS neurons is required for entering REMs.
source: This finding suggests that a minimal activity of TMNHIS neurons is required for entering REMs, and suppression of TMNHIS activity therefore likely facilitates transitions to REMs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TMNHIS activity reaches its lowest level at REMs onset.

claim: Suppression of TMNHIS activity likely facilitates transitions to REMs.
source: This finding suggests that a minimal activity of TMNHIS neurons is required for entering REMs, and suppression of TMNHIS activity therefore likely facilitates transitions to REMs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TMNHIS activity reaches its lowest level at REMs onset.

claim: SwiChR++-mediated inhibition of POAGAD2→TMN neurons reduced the amount of REMs compared with recordings without laser stimulation in the same mice and eYFP mice with laser stimulation.
source: SwiChR++-mediated inhibition of POAGAD2→TMN neurons reduced the amount of REMs compared with recordings without laser stimulation in the same mice and eYFP mice with laser stimulation (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic inhibition data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: The overall time spent in wake and NREMs was not altered by SwiChR++-mediated inhibition of POAGAD2→TMN neurons.
source: The overall time spent in wake and NREMs was not altered by SwiChR++-mediated inhibition (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B), suggesting that POAGAD2→TMN neuron activity specifically regulates the amount of REMs.
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic inhibition data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: POAGAD2→TMN neuron activity specifically regulates the amount of REMs.
source: The overall time spent in wake and NREMs was not altered by SwiChR++-mediated inhibition (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B), suggesting that POAGAD2→TMN neuron activity specifically regulates the amount of REMs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that inhibition only affected REMs and not wake or NREMs.

claim: SwiChR++-mediated inhibition of POAGAD2→TMN neurons increased the δ and σ power in the EEG during REMs compared with SwiChR++-without laser and eYFP-laser groups.
source: During REMs, SwiChR++-mediated inhibition of POAGAD2→TMN neurons increased the δ and σ power in the EEG compared with SwiChR++-without laser and eYFP-laser groups (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by EEG spectral analysis shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There were no differences in the amount of REMs, NREMs, and wake between SwiChR++ and eYFP groups during the post-laser recordings.
source: Despite the reduction of REMs during the laser stimulation in SwiChR++ mice (Figure 2C), there were no differences in the amount of REMs, NREMs, and wake between SwiChR++ and eYFP groups during the post-laser recordings (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F), suggesting that the loss of REMs during SwiChR++-mediated inhibition was not followed by a homeostatic increase in REMs.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from post-laser recordings shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: The loss of REMs during SwiChR++-mediated inhibition was not followed by a homeostatic increase in REMs.
source: Despite the reduction of REMs during the laser stimulation in SwiChR++ mice (Figure 2C), there were no differences in the amount of REMs, NREMs, and wake between SwiChR++ and eYFP groups during the post-laser recordings (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F), suggesting that the loss of REMs during SwiChR++-mediated inhibition was not followed by a homeostatic increase in REMs.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of rebound in REMs after inhibition.

claim: SwiChR++-mediated inhibition of TMNHIS neurons increased the amount of REMs compared with recordings without laser stimulation in the same mice and eYFP mice with laser stimulation.
source: SwiChR++-mediated inhibition of TMNHIS neurons increased the amount of REMs compared with recordings without laser stimulation in the same mice and eYFP mice with laser stimulation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic inhibition data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: 6 hr of REMs restriction significantly reduced the amount of REMs and duration of REMs episodes, while increasing their frequency.
source: Compared with the baseline recordings from the same mice during the same circadian time, we found that 6 hr of REMs restriction (ZT 1.5–7.5) significantly reduced the amount of REMs and duration of REMs episodes, while increasing their frequency (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, D-F; amount: Cohen's d [d]=–1.621; duration: d=–2.669; frequency: d=1.294).
evidence: This claim is supported by REMs restriction data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, D-F.

claim: The number of motor activations gradually increased as mice tried to enter REMs more frequently, indicating the accumulation of REMs pressure.
source: The number of motor activations gradually increased as mice tried to enter REMs more frequently, indicating the accumulation of REMs pressure (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data on motor activations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: During rebound, the amount of REMs was significantly increased compared with that during the same circadian time due to an increased frequency of REMs episodes.
source: During rebound (ZT 7.5–8.5), the amount of REMs was significantly increased compared with that during the same circadian time due to an increased frequency of REMs episodes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H-K; amount: d=0.868; frequency: d=1.147), compensating for the amount of REMs lost during restriction.
evidence: This claim is supported by REMs rebound data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H-K.

claim: During restriction, the number of calcium transients of the POAGAD2→TMN neurons was significantly increased compared with that during baseline recordings.
source: During restriction, the number of calcium transients of the POAGAD2→TMN neurons was significantly increased compared with that during baseline recordings (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data during REMs restriction shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The number of calcium peaks in POAGAD2→TMN neurons was significantly elevated during NREMs during REMs restriction.
source: In particular, the number of calcium peaks was significantly elevated during NREMs, likely reflecting an increased pressure to transition to REMs (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: During REMs restriction, the amplitude of NREMs and REMs calcium transients in POAGAD2→TMN neurons was significantly higher compared with that during the circadian baseline.
source: During REMs restriction, the amplitude of NREMs and REMs calcium transients was significantly higher compared with that during the circadian baseline (Figure 3D and E) and remained elevated during NREMs in the rebound phase (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: The amplitude of calcium transients in POAGAD2→TMN neurons remained elevated during NREMs in the rebound phase.
source: During REMs restriction, the amplitude of NREMs and REMs calcium transients was significantly higher compared with that during the circadian baseline (Figure 3D and E) and remained elevated during NREMs in the rebound phase (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: During periods of high REMs pressure, the POAGAD2→TMN neurons exhibit an increased number of calcium transients with higher amplitude compared with that during baseline levels.
source: Overall, these findings show that during periods of high REMs pressure, the POAGAD2→TMN neurons exhibit an increased number of calcium transients with higher amplitude compared with that during baseline levels suggesting that the activity of these neurons may reflect the heightened homeostatic need for REMs.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from Figure 3.

claim: The activity of POAGAD2→TMN neurons may reflect the heightened homeostatic need for REMs.
source: Overall, these findings show that during periods of high REMs pressure, the POAGAD2→TMN neurons exhibit an increased number of calcium transients with higher amplitude compared with that during baseline levels suggesting that the activity of these neurons may reflect the heightened homeostatic need for REMs.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between increased calcium transients and REMs pressure.

claim: SwiChR-mediated inhibition of POAGAD2→TMN neurons during REMs restriction decreased the percentage of REMs and reduced the frequency of REMs episodes with marginal significance.
source: During restriction, SwiChR-mediated inhibition of POAGAD2→TMN neurons decreased the percentage of REMs and reduced the frequency of REMs episodes with marginal significance (Figure 4B–D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B amount: d=–1.254).
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic inhibition data during REMs restriction shown in Figure 4B–D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Inhibition of POAGAD2→TMN neurons during REMs restriction resulted in a reduced amount of REMs during the rebound compared with that in eYFP mice.
source: We found that inhibition of POAGAD2→TMN neurons during REMs restriction resulted in a reduced amount of REMs during the rebound compared with that in eYFP mice (Figure 4B, F, and G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, E, amount: d=–1.317).
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic inhibition data shown in Figure 4B, F, and G, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, E.

claim: Inactivating POAGAD2→TMN neurons during heightened REMs pressure not only decreased the amount of REMs, but also prevented its homeostatic rebound during the following recovery sleep.
source: Thus, inactivating POAGAD2→TMN neurons during heightened REMs pressure not only decreased the amount of REMs, but also prevented its homeostatic rebound during the following recovery sleep.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from Figure 4.

claim: Inhibition of POAGAD2→TMN neurons during REMs restriction reduced the REMs δ power, NREMs θ and σ power compared with that in eYFP mice with laser stimulation.
source: We found that inhibition of POAGAD2→TMN neurons during REMs restriction reduced the REMs δ power, NREMs θ and σ power compared with that in eYFP mice with laser stimulation (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by EEG spectral analysis shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The reduced θ and σ power during NREMs could result from less attempts to enter REMs.
source: The reduced θ and σ power during NREMs could result from less attempts to enter REMs (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is inferred from the relationship between EEG power and REMs attempts.

claim: Inhibiting POAGAD2→TMN neurons during REMs restriction significantly decreased the amount of REMs and blocked the subsequent rebound in REMs.
source: Taken together, inhibiting POAGAD2→TMN neurons during REMs restriction significantly decreased the amount of REMs and blocked the subsequent rebound in REMs.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from Figure 4.

claim: The heightened activity of POAGAD2→TMN neurons during sleep encodes the increased need for REMs and consequently plays an important role in the homeostatic response to REMs restriction.
source: Our data suggest that the heightened activity of POAGAD2→TMN neurons during sleep encodes the increased need for REMs and consequently plays an important role in the homeostatic response to REMs restriction.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined findings of increased activity during restriction and blocked rebound upon inhibition.

claim: POAGAD2→TMN neurons become activated throughout NREMs before transitioning to REMs, while being most active during REMs.
source: Using fiber photometry, we showed that the POAGAD2→TMN neurons become activated throughout NREMs before transitioning to REMs, while being most active during REMs (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Figure 1.

claim: Sustained optogenetic inhibition of POAGAD2→TMN neurons reduced the overall amount of REMs, and the loss of REMs was not compensated during the subsequent recovery sleep.
source: Sustained optogenetic inhibition of POAGAD2→TMN neurons reduced the overall amount of REMs, and the loss of REMs was not compensated during the subsequent recovery sleep (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Figure 2.

claim: During the period of high REMs pressure, POAGAD2→TMN neurons exhibited an increased number of calcium transients with elevated amplitude.
source: During the period of high REMs pressure, POAGAD2→TMN neurons exhibited an increased number of calcium transients with elevated amplitude (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Figure 3.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of POAGAD2→TMN neurons during REMs restriction attenuated the subsequent rebound of REMs.
source: Optogenetic inhibition of POAGAD2→TMN neurons during REMs restriction attenuated the subsequent rebound of REMs (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Figure 4.

claim: The activity of POAGAD2→TMN neurons reflects an increased need for REMs in the form of enhanced calcium transients and is required for the rebound following the loss of REMs.
source: Our results suggest that the activity of POAGAD2→TMN neurons reflects an increased need for REMs in the form of enhanced calcium transients and is required for the rebound following the loss of REMs.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined findings of the study.

claim: The TMN contains histamine-producing neurons.
source: The TMN contains histamine-producing neurons and antagonizing histamine signaling causes sleepiness (Watanabe et al., 1983; Panula et al., 1984; Lin et al., 1988; Bayliss et al., 1990; Haas et al., 2008; Uygun et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Antagonizing histamine signaling causes sleepiness.
source: The TMN contains histamine-producing neurons and antagonizing histamine signaling causes sleepiness (Watanabe et al., 1983; Panula et al., 1984; Lin et al., 1988; Bayliss et al., 1990; Haas et al., 2008; Uygun et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: TMNHIS neurons are most active during wakefulness and less active during NREMs and REMs.
source: Consistent with our photometry recordings (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), electrophysiological recordings demonstrate that TMNHIS neurons are most active during wakefulness and less active during NREMs and REMs (Steininger et al., 1999; Vanni-Mercier et al., 2003; John et al., 2004; Takahashi et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research and data from the current study.

claim: Mutual inhibition between TMNHIS and POAGAD2→TMN neurons may explain their antagonistic activity pattern revealed in fiber photometry recordings.
source: Mutual inhibition between TMNHIS and POAGAD2→TMN neurons may explain their antagonistic activity pattern revealed in our fiber photometry recordings.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed activity patterns and known connectivity.

claim: The majority of sleep-active neurons in the POA are most active during REMs.
source: While many studies have focused on the role of the POA in regulating NREMs (Sherin et al., 1996; Szymusiak et al., 1998; Lu et al., 2000; Zhang et al., 2015; Kroeger et al., 2018; Ma et al., 2019), previous in vivo electrophysiological studies found that the majority of sleep-active neurons in the POA are most active during REMs (Osaka and Matsumura, 1995; Takahashi et al., 2009; Antila et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: GABAergic neurons in the POA and their subtypes expressing cholecystokinin, corticotropin-releasing hormone, tachykinin 1, or galanin are most active during REMs.
source: Similarly, recent fiber photometry recordings demonstrated that GABAergic neurons in the POA and their subtypes expressing cholecystokinin, corticotropin-releasing hormone, tachykinin 1, or galanin are most active during REMs (Miracca et al., 2022; Smith et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Deleting the NMDA receptor GluN1 subunit in the POA reduced REMs.
source: Deleting the NMDA receptor GluN1 subunit in the POA reduced REMs (Miracca et al., 2022), and in line with this, sustained optogenetic inhibition of POAGAD2→TMN neurons specifically decreased REMs.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The number of c-Fos positive POA neurons is positively correlated with the amount of REMs in rats.
source: A previous study showed that the number of c-Fos positive POA neurons is positively correlated with the amount of REMs in rats (Lu et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: REMs restriction led to an increase in the number of POA neurons expressing c-Fos, which was correlated with the number of attempts to enter REMs.
source: Moreover, REMs restriction led to an increase in the number of POA neurons expressing c-Fos, which was correlated with the number of attempts to enter REMs (Gvilia et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The POA is crucial for the homeostatic regulation of REMs.
source: Together with our findings that the number of calcium transients of POAGAD2→TMN neurons increased during REMs restriction and that inhibition of these neurons blocked the following REMs rebound, these results support a crucial role of the POA in the homeostatic regulation of REMs.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined findings of the study and prior research.

claim: POA neurons projecting to REMs-regulatory pontine regions including the laterodorsal tegmental nucleus, locus coeruleus (LC), and dorsal raphe nucleus express increased levels of c-Fos after periods of dark exposure that increased REMs.
source: A previous study showed that POA neurons projecting to REMs-regulatory pontine regions including the laterodorsal tegmental nucleus, locus coeruleus (LC), and dorsal raphe nucleus express increased levels of c-Fos after periods of dark exposure that increased REMs (Lu et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The number of c-Fos positive POA neurons projecting to the LC was not increased upon REMs restriction, suggesting that this subpopulation may not be involved in the homeostatic regulation of REMs.
source: However, the number of c-Fos positive POA neurons projecting to the LC was not increased upon REMs restriction, suggesting that this subpopulation may not be involved in the homeostatic regulation of REMs (Verret et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research and includes an inference.

claim: The POA also projects to other REMs-regulatory regions such as the ventrolateral periaqueductal gray (vlPAG) and lateral hypothalamus.
source: Besides the TMN, the POA also projects to other REMs-regulatory regions such as the ventrolateral periaqueductal gray (vlPAG) and lateral hypothalamus (Steininger et al., 2001; Saito et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: GABAergic neurons in the vlPAG have been previously implicated in the homeostatic regulation of REMs.
source: Particularly, the projections to the vlPAG are of interest for future research, as GABAergic neurons in this area have been previously implicated in the homeostatic regulation of REMs (Hayashi et al., 2015; Weber et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Sleep-promoting neurons in the dorsal fan-shaped body of Drosophila display increased intrinsic neuronal excitability in response to sleep need.
source: Sleep-promoting neurons in the dorsal fan-shaped body of Drosophila display increased intrinsic neuronal excitability in response to sleep need (Donlea et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: REMs deprivation was shown to change the intrinsic excitability of hippocampal neurons and impact synaptic plasticity.
source: REMs deprivation was shown to change the intrinsic excitability of hippocampal neurons and impact synaptic plasticity (McDermott et al., 2003; Mallick and Singh, 2011; Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The elevated activity of POAGAD2→TMN neurons during heightened REMs pressure may be the result of an increased excitability.
source: The elevated activity of POAGAD2→TMN neurons during heightened REMs pressure may similarly be the result of an increased excitability.
evidence: This is speculated based on findings in other systems.

claim: The POA is also involved in the homeostatic regulation of NREMs.
source: Given that the POA is also involved in the homeostatic regulation of NREMs (Sherin et al., 1996; Szymusiak et al., 1998; Gong et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2015; Ma et al., 2019; Lu et al., 2000), it would be interesting to study how different POA subpopulations integrate the homeostatic need for NREMs and REMs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: REMs disturbances are observed in a variety of psychiatric disorders such as depression and PTSD and often precede their clinical onset.
source: REMs disturbances are observed in a variety of psychiatric disorders such as depression and PTSD and often precede their clinical onset (Ross et al., 1989; Gottesmann and Gottesman, 2007; Germain, 2013; Palagini et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Elucidating the circuit mechanisms underlying the homeostatic regulation of REMs may provide novel therapeutic targets to specifically regulate and normalize REMs in psychiatric disorders.
source: Elucidating the circuit mechanisms underlying the homeostatic regulation of REMs may provide novel therapeutic targets to specifically regulate and normalize REMs in these psychiatric disorders to alleviate associated symptoms and potentially slow down their progression.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future applications.

claim: Virus expression and optic fiber tracts were located in the ventrolateral POA, lateral POA, and the lateral part of medial POA.
source: pGP-AAV-Syn-FLEX-jGCaMP8s-WPRE was developed from the GENIE Project (Zhang et al., 2023) (162377-AAVrg, Addgene). pAAV-Syn-FLEX-GCaMP6s-WPRE-SV40 was developed from Douglas Kim & GENIE Project (Chen et al., 2013) (Penn Vector Core or 100845-AAV1, Addgene).
evidence: This describes the anatomical location of experimental manipulations.

claim: The automatic brain state classification algorithm has 90.256% accuracy compared with manual scoring by expert annotators.
source: Our automatic algorithm that has been previously used in Weber et al., 2015; Weber et al., 2018; Chung et al., 2017; Antila et al., 2022; Smith et al., 2024; Stucynski et al., 2022; Schott et al., 2023, has 90.256% accuracy compared with the manual scoring by expert annotators.
evidence: This is a validation of the methodology used in the study.
